newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish yields seen up on mkt rate rise potential.
newsitem.headline: Polish yields seen up on mkt rate rise potential.

text.p: The increased likelihood of an interest rate rise to counter monetary growth from the planned 1.9 percent budget gap next year should boost yields of Polish T-bills at the Monday primary tender, dealers said.

The central bank has said the planned gap, instead of a balanced budget, made a rate rise more likely because otherwise the extra government spending would increase the already high domestic demand and dangerously widen the trade gap.

The National Bank of Poland would like to see a 1.5 percent deficit at the highest while the Polish Peasant Party, the junior partner in the ruling coalition with the ex-communists, wants a larger deficit than the finance ministry's 1.9 percent.
"The planned deficit is likely to lead to a rate rise so yields may go strongly up at the primary tender," said Piotr Broda, T-bill dealer at Creditanstalt in Warsaw.

"Foreign players are already selling Polish paper after the NBP remarks on the rate rise, but there is not much demand on the secondary market and yields of T-bills and two-year fixed bonds went sharply up," he said.

Dealers said demand at the 1.2 billion zloty tender was not likely to exceed 400 million zlotys with the 52-week maximum yield, up 21.85-90 from 21.77 percent at the last tender, the 26-week bills up to 21.75-80 from 21.64 and 13-week paper up to 21.30-50 from 21.13 percent.
"There isn't going to be any demand from foreign players. They are now doing right the opposite -- selling," said Robert Gluch, T-bill dealer at ING Bank in Warsaw.

Dealers estimated foreigners have sold 500 million zlotys of T-bills over the last two weeks, since the deficit dispute started with NBP remarks that the lack of a balanced budget next year may in the future lead to a Czech style crisis.
Dealers said that despite the rather bearish foreign investor mood, the zloty was likely to stay within a 0.8-0.5 percent range above the trading band centre next week.

"Foreign players start buying the zloty when it falls to 0.5 percent above parity and sell it when it firms to about 0.8 percent so it might stay in that range next week," said Mateusz Bieniek, forex dealer at Societe Generale in Warsaw.
The zloty closed at 0.73/0.71 percent on Friday, down from 1.08/0.97 percent a week ago. It was at 3.2950/55 against the dollar and 1.8798/03 against the mark.
Dealers said the money market had already priced in the potential rate rise with one to three month deposist rising 0.5 point since the Thursday NBP statement to 22.8 percent at bid.
"The NBP remarks did the trick -- deposit rates across the range have moved up and are likely to stay high for next week," said Malgorzata Sikora, deposit dealer at ING Bank.
Dealers said the rise of the maximum yield of the central bank's 182-day bills by 0.25 point to 22.25 percent at today's tender clearly signalled market rates were goining up.
"All we have to wait for now is the new reverse repo rate," said Piotr Korcz, T-bill dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.
The central bank has been offering 300 million zloty reverse repos for three days in a row now, but the tight market offered either no bids at all or just a fraction of the offer.
